Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Elena Martinez remembered the afternoon she was twelve when the air in the kitchen shifted. Her father had been quiet for hours, but the clink of his coffee cup against the counter had been too sharp, and when he turned, his face was already tight. She watched his hands flex before he pushed her against the cabinets, a sudden, heavy shove that left her breathless. That was how it always began: without warning, the domestic space turning into a place where she had to brace herself. Over the years, she learned to anticipate the sudden shifts in tone, moving through the house like a ghost. When the shouting started, she would lock her bedroom door and press her back against the wall, counting the floorboards until his footsteps faded. She had come to believe that safety was a myth and that control was the only thing she could actually hold. Those early lessons bled into adulthood. Elena trained as a physical therapist, drawn to the predictability of anatomy. Yet the clinic became a landscape of unspoken threats. She positioned her evaluation table so its back rested against the brick wall, and when patients entered her room, she kept a wary eye on their approach. She found herself scanning hallways for anyone moving too quickly, her shoulders tightening the moment a stranger closed the distance, even a colleague offering a casual hello. Between patients, she wiped down surfaces, aligned resistance bands, stacked chart folders until they formed perfect columns. The rhythm grounded her. If she could make the environment orderly, she reasoned, she could keep the sudden from happening. During long shifts, when the weight of the day pressed against her ribs, she would retreat to the break room and eat until the hollow ache in her stomach filled with something heavier. She avoided phone calls, skipped team meetings, and told herself she was just too busy, though the truth was simpler: she could not bear the unpredictable. Now divorced, she found herself alone with the quiet. Memories of her childhood did not arrive as a single story. Sometimes, years later, she would recount the violence in a flat voice, feeling nothing as if she were reading someone else’s transcript. Other times, a smell of burnt coffee or the scuff of a dress shoe would pull a sudden, fragmented image to the surface—the glare of a lightbulb, the sharp angle of a wrist—and then it would slip away, leaving her wondering if she had imagined it. The events felt so extreme she often doubted they had truly happened. At night, the quiet turned against her. She would wake with a start, heart hammering, convinced the door was unlocked. She would get up, check the locks three times, press her spine against the bedroom wall, and wait for her breathing to slow. By morning, the dread had settled into her bones. For weeks, Elena had pushed through, telling herself it was just aging. But lately, the routines had begun to fail. One Tuesday, after she had avoided a routine follow-up with a regular patient because the lobby felt too crowded, she found herself sitting in her car outside a community mental health center. She had come to believe she was breaking, that the careful architecture of her days was finally collapsing. She wanted the fear to stop, to work a full day without bracing, to remember her childhood without a wall between her and it. She took a breath, turned off the engine, and walked through the doors.
